Currently the problem is this:

  1. Company A is consumer-hostile, committing to price fixing and dumping.

  2. People support small company B instead which has more consumer-friendly practices. Company B still makes profit.

  3. Company A acquires company B for some amount of money to get rid of competition.

  4. Now consumers have to put up with company A.

What kind of a regulation would prevent these things from happening? Current regulations, if present, work only on monopolies but not against things like fictional work monopolies.
If you had to make a regulation that would protect consumers against company mergers and acquisations, how would you make that work?

If competition is removed because of the merger then they shouldn't be allowed to merge. If by not merging the smaller company goes out of business then the larger company needs to be broken up (like Ma Bell in the 80s).

Market share needs to be looked at. Companies that have a majority of market share (greater than 40% or some other value) should not be allowed to merge with another company to increase its market share.

I suppose some research should be done as far as seeing how much market share a company can acquire before monopolistic tendencies (like price fixing, supplying inferior products, lack of innovation) take over. Whatever number that is, then that is the maximum amount of market share a company would be allowed to provide for the public.
If there are less than 10 competitors in the markets served by Company A, they aren't allowed to purchase/merge with a competitor that serves those markets.

I think this question exposes one major issue, and peculiarity, of capitalism. Take a normal competitive venture like sports. It's really easy to go from nobody to advanced beginner. But it gets harder and harder to achieve more the bigger you get. By the time you start reaching professional level gains that would be negligible at most other levels suddenly become monumental. A world class swimmer speeding up his laps by half a second would be an unbelievable achievement whereas a beginner speeding up their laps by seconds is pretty standard.

Now back to capitalism. The strange thing is that the bigger you get the easier it gets to get even bigger. Consume more companies and your growth and margins grows ever larger. That growth enables you to consume even more and grow even larger, faster. This is why never ending exponential growth is considered a reasonable goal even for the largest companies in the world. Imagine if a world class basketball player could somehow 'consumer' another player and obtain their skills. It'd turn the sport into a cannibalistic shit show, and that's what we have in the market today.

And there is no solution here. The lack of competition is a tertiary issue to the problem that growth becomes easier the bigger you get. For instance take Time Warner and Comcast. Very few people really find the service or price these companies offer desirable, but they're able to destroy all competition by nature of their size alone. And as they grow ever larger and more powerful, they're able to destroy competition even more effectively. And now on the topic of mergers. These two companies are effectively splitting up the country and systematically destroying competition region by region. However, they refuse to compete or try to do this against one another. They're not legally merged, but they're for all intents and purpose working exactly like merged companies would. At this point, merging would be more of a formality than anything else.

Actually there is one solution, but it's one that very few people in the current American zeitgeist would be willing to support. The issue is that the bigger you grow, the easier it is to grow even larger. So the solution is to start slowing down growth at extreme levels. One way to do this would be taxation. Companies that net less than $100k pay 0% in tax. The tax on $100k to $1,000,000 is set to 20% and on upwards. Set the taxation on profit for companies earning billions of dollars to new ceilings. The 60s was an era of tremendous growth for the US, yet the nominal tax rate max was set at 91%. Go figure. There would undoubtedly be tax avoidance schemes that would need to be countermanded, but the issue is that growth needs to be slowed down instead of accelerated as companies grow larger.

It is difficult to protect consumers through competition regulation. When a large competitor lowers prices to at or below cost to drive competitors under, then establish monopoly dominance - the purpose is to be in a position to raise prices in a captive market. Regulating this behavior in the past has proven to be of questionable benefit at best... because it is not a simple thing to regulate. How do you judge at what price point the selling of goods is harmful vrs of economic benefit. This can only ever be an arbitrary call - and is often as not the wrong call.

In my own opinion, the best way to control this behavior is to minimize barriers to entry into the markets as much as possible. For example, the broad band infrastructure in Ontario is controlled by a small handful of companies - very close to total monopolies - however, laws provide for smaller carriers to lease access on this infrastructure at bulk discount wholesale rates - which provides a robust market of highly competitive ISP's in Ontario. The big carriers still have their infrastructure earning money, but they are not able to behave as complete monopolists likely would if the smaller carriers were not in the game.

So this regulation approach creates entry into the market for smaller firms - and that creates competition where natural barriers would otherwise prevent it. Also - the smaller firms do not have to build the tech infrastructure which only very large firms have to capacity to provide. Regulating a single bulk price point for all of the smaller competitors is far easier than trying to assess fair vrs unfair on a case by case basis. You use the regulation to set up the boundaries of the sandbox - inside the sandbox it's anything goes.

If your barriers to entry are low, then in the case put forth by the OP above - you simply start a new company if Company A starts to raise prices as a monopolist.

As much as possible - it is better to regulate the environment within which the companies operate - rather than the individual companies themselves.
